cardUpdates.answerEn: a framework that multiplies estimated factors to approximate how many extraterrestrial civilizations might communicate in the Milky Way
cardUpdates.noteEn: Astronomer Frank Drake introduced the framework in 1961. Its factors concern stars, planets, life, intelligence, communication, and how long detectable civilizations last; their uncertain values make the result an estimate, not a measured count.

cardUpdates.answerEn: broken
cardUpdates.noteEn: Romper means “to break.” Its completed-action form is irregular: romper becomes roto, not rompido. After a helper such as ha, roto stays unchanged: ha roto, “has broken.” When it describes a broken thing, its ending matches that thing: un vaso roto, una taza rota.

cardUpdates.answerEn: some; an unspecified one
cardUpdates.noteEn: Alguno loses its final o directly before a noun for one thing that uses el, such as libro: alguno becomes algún libro. This shortened form keeps its stress on the final syllable, written with an accent on ú. It does not identify which particular person or thing.

example.en: Some neighbor will have the key.

cardUpdates.answerEn: any; an unspecified one (in a question)
cardUpdates.noteEn: Alguno loses its final o directly before a noun for one thing that uses el, such as problema: alguno becomes algún problema. The accent on ú keeps the stress on the final syllable. In a question about whether one exists, English often uses “any.”

cardUpdates.answerEn: same
cardUpdates.noteEn: Misma identifies the identical one, not a different one. Its ending matches a noun that uses la: la misma ruta. A noun that uses el instead takes mismo: el mismo camino. For more than one, add s: las mismas rutas.

cardUpdates.answerEn: right?; isn’t that so?
cardUpdates.noteEn: Put ¿verdad? after a statement when you expect it to be correct and ask the listener to confirm it. The word stays the same whether the statement is positive or negative and whoever it is about.

example.en: You already have the key, right?

cardUpdates.answerEn: I try; I attempt
parts; areas
there was; there were
cardUpdates.noteEn: Había says that something existed or was present in a past setting. It stays the same before one thing or several: había una silla, había dos sillas. This is different from había meaning “had” before another verb's completed-action form.

cardUpdates.answerEn: where
cardUpdates.noteEn: Dónde keeps its written accent when asking about a place, whether the question stands alone or sits inside another sentence: ¿Dónde vive Ana? and No sé dónde vive Ana. Unaccented donde connects to a place without asking a question.

example.es: No recuerdo dónde dejé las llaves.
example.en: I don't remember where I left the keys.

cardUpdates.answerEn: is pleasing; like(s)
cardUpdates.noteEn: Gusta expresses liking, but the thing or activity that is liked controls its form. Use gusta for one thing or an activity, and gustan for several things. A short word identifies who likes it: me means to me, te to you, and le or les to another person or people.

example.es: A mis vecinos les gusta caminar.

cardUpdates.answerEn: you have (a special form of tener)
cardUpdates.noteEn: Tengas is a form of tener, “to have,” for tú, one familiar person. Certain surrounding expressions require tengas instead of the ordinary tienes: puede que tengas presents a possibility, and es bueno que tengas gives an evaluation.

cardUpdates.answerEn: did; would do or make (a special past form of hacer)
cardUpdates.noteEn: Hiciera is a form of hacer, “to do or make.” Some expressions about a purpose or an open possibility require hiciera instead of the ordinary past forms hice or hizo. Hiciera can refer to I, he, she, or formal you; the surrounding words identify who. Its English wording depends on that surrounding expression.

example.es: Le di papel para que hiciera un dibujo.
example.en: I gave him paper so that he could make a drawing.

cardUpdates.answerEn: wants; wants to
cardUpdates.noteEn: Quiere is a present form of querer, “to want.” It can describe he, she, or one person addressed formally as usted. With se, it can describe what people in general want. Before an action, use the action verb's unchanged dictionary form, such as descansar, “to rest.”

example.en: Would you like to rest, ma'am?

cardUpdates.answerEn: geeks; nerds
cardUpdates.noteEn: An informal plural word for enthusiasts with intense or specialized interests. Depending on tone, it can be affectionate or mocking.

example.es: Mis amigos son frikis del cine.

cardUpdates.answerEn: much; far (strengthening a comparison)
cardUpdates.noteEn: Put mucho before a comparison such as mejor, “better,” or más, “more,” to make the difference stronger. Mucho stays unchanged in this use. Use mucho mejor, not muy mejor.

example.es: Este camino es mucho más corto.

cardUpdates.answerEn: wanted; meant to
cardUpdates.noteEn: Quería is a past form of querer, “to want.” It describes a wish or intention at that past time without saying whether it was fulfilled. The same form can refer to I, he, she, or formal you; context identifies the person.

example.es: Quería comprar pan, pero la tienda estaba cerrada.
example.en: I wanted to buy bread, but the shop was closed.

cardUpdates.answerEn: remain; are left
cardUpdates.noteEn: Quedan says that several things remain. Use queda for one thing and quedan for more than one. A short word such as me, te, or les can identify who has them left; the number of remaining things, not the number of people, controls queda or quedan.

cardUpdates.answerEn: doing; making
cardUpdates.noteEn: Haciendo is the unchanged -iendo action form of hacer, “to do or make.” With a form of estar, it describes an action in progress. Without estar, it can describe how another action happens or an activity happening at the same time. The surrounding construction supplies meanings such as English “by.”

cardUpdates.answerEn: discovered; found
cardUpdates.noteEn: Descubierto is the irregular completed-action form of descubrir, “to discover”; it is not descubrido. After haber, the helping verb meaning “have” or “had,” it stays unchanged: han descubierto, “they have discovered.” With ser in a description meaning “was discovered,” it matches the thing: el lugar fue descubierto, but la isla fue descubierta.

cardUpdates.answerEn: interesting
cardUpdates.noteEn: Interesante can describe a stated noun or a noun that is understood from context. In una interesante, English adds “an interesting one,” but Spanish leaves out the repeated noun. Interesante stays the same for masculine and feminine; interesantes is plural.

example.es: Busco una novela; quiero una interesante.
example.en: I'm looking for a novel; I want an interesting one.

cardUpdates.answerEn: lower (plural)
cardUpdates.noteEn: Inferiores describes more than one thing as lower. With los or las and an understood noun, English may add “ones”: los inferiores means the lower ones. The describing word has the same form for masculine and feminine; inferior is singular.

cardUpdates.answerEn: wow; oh my
cardUpdates.noteEn: As an exclamation, vaya can express surprise, admiration, or annoyance. This use is separate from vaya as a form of ir, “to go.”

cardUpdates.answerEn: something; anything
cardUpdates.noteEn: Algo refers to an unspecified thing. English often uses “anything” in a question even though Spanish still uses algo. It does not change for the thing's gender or number.

cardUpdates.answerEn: true; correct
cardUpdates.noteEn: Cierto can describe a claim as true or stand alone as a short response agreeing with it. This differs from cierto before a noun meaning “a certain.”

cardUpdates.answerEn: to go out; to come out; to exit
cardUpdates.noteEn: Salir describes movement from inside to outside. English chooses “come out” or “go out” according to the speaker's viewpoint.

example.es: El perro quiere salir del coche.
example.en: The dog wants to get out of the car.

cardUpdates.answerEn: Earth; the planet Earth
flow; sequence through a process
cardUpdates.noteEn: Flujo can describe the path and order followed by steps in a process, including the instructions in a program. This use is not a stream of data or the physical flow of a liquid.

example.es: Una decisión cambia el flujo del trabajo.

cardUpdates.answerEn: all; everyone (the whole understood group)
cardUpdates.noteEn: Todos can stand for all the people or things in an understood group. Other words show whether English needs “all of us,” “all of them,” or “everyone.” Use todos for masculine or mixed groups and todas for an all-feminine group.

cardUpdates.answerEn: one (feminine)
cardUpdates.noteEn: Una counts one feminine thing or occasion. Use un before a masculine noun and una before a feminine noun: un libro, una página. In una vez, una still gives the number one; vez supplies “time” or “occasion.”

cardUpdates.answerEn: no; not
only; just
do; does; indeed (emphasizing a positive statement)
cardUpdates.noteEn: Before a verb, sí stresses that something really happens or is true, often correcting a negative idea. It can also appear as sí que before the verb. Keep the written accent: si without an accent means “if.”

example.en: I don't sing, but I do dance.

cardUpdates.answerEn: nice; lovely; neat
cardUpdates.noteEn: Bonito gives a positive evaluation of something pleasing or impressive. It can describe a noun or stand alone as an approving reaction. When it describes a noun, its ending matches: bonito, bonita, bonitos, bonitas.

cardUpdates.answerEn: are (a place or condition)
cardUpdates.noteEn: Están is a form of estar for they or plural you, ustedes. It describes where people or things are, or their condition. Spanish often leaves out the separate word for they or you because the context identifies them. Before another verb's ongoing-action form, están has a different helping-verb use.

example.es: Las maletas están junto a la puerta.
example.en: The suitcases are beside the door.

cardUpdates.answerEn: test; check
good (feminine singular)
cardUpdates.noteEn: Buena is the feminine form of bueno, “good.” Use it for one feminine noun: una buena pregunta; for more than one, use buenas preguntas.

example.es: La biblioteca tiene una buena colección.
example.en: The library has a good collection.

cardUpdates.answerEn: uh; um
cardUpdates.noteEn: A hesitation sound used while the speaker pauses to think or find words. This is different from eh used to call for attention or ask for agreement.

cardUpdates.answerEn: normal; usual; ordinary
is; are (a place or condition)
cardUpdates.noteEn: Está is a form of estar for he, she, it, or one person addressed formally as usted. It describes where someone or something is, or their condition. The surrounding words identify the person; Spanish need not add a separate word for he, she, it, or formal you.

cardUpdates.answerEn: to be (a place or condition)
cardUpdates.noteEn: Estar is the unchanged dictionary form used to describe a location or condition. In quiero estar, “I want to be,” quiero changes for the person and time, while estar stays unchanged.

example.es: Quiero estar cerca de la ventana.
example.en: I want to be near the window.

cardUpdates.answerEn: there is; there are
cardUpdates.noteEn: Hay introduces what exists, is present, or is available. It stays unchanged for one thing or several: hay una tienda, hay dos tiendas. English changes 'there is' to 'there are,' but Spanish does not change hay. The English 'there' in this pattern does not point to a place. Inside a description such as la tienda que hay aquí, English can instead say 'the shop that is here'; Spanish hay still introduces what is present.

cardUpdates.answerEn: to work; to run; to function
cardUpdates.noteEn: Ir can describe how a system, machine, or process works rather than movement to a place. A following description says how it is running: ir bien, “to work well,” or ir lento, “to run slowly.”

example.es: El ordenador debería ir más rápido.

cardUpdates.answerEn: to go out (socially)
cardUpdates.noteEn: Ir can refer to a social outing in expressions such as ir de marcha, going out to party, or ir de copas, going out for drinks. Ir is the unchanged dictionary form; changed forms include voy, “I go,” and vamos, “we go.”

example.es: Queremos ir de copas el viernes.
example.en: We want to go out for drinks on Friday.

cardUpdates.answerEn: we are (in a place or time)
cardUpdates.noteEn: Estamos is the form of estar for nosotros, “we.” It can place the group somewhere, as in estamos aquí, or place us in a period, as in estamos en junio. This is different from estamos helping another verb describe an action in progress.

cardUpdates.answerEn: we are (helping describe an action in progress)
cardUpdates.noteEn: Estamos is the form of estar for nosotros, “we.” Before an ongoing-action form, usually ending in -ando or -iendo, it says that the group is doing that action now or during the period being discussed.

cardUpdates.answerEn: was (a past place, condition, or situation)
cardUpdates.noteEn: Estaba is a past form of estar. It describes a location or condition at a past time without by itself marking when that situation began or ended. The same form can refer to I, he, she, it, or formal you; the surrounding words identify who.

cardUpdates.answerEn: was; were (helping describe an action in progress in the past)
cardUpdates.noteEn: Estaba is a past form of estar for I, he, she, it, or formal you. Before an ongoing-action form, usually ending in -ando or -iendo, it presents an action as in progress at a past time.

cardUpdates.answerEn: I left (something in a condition)
cardUpdates.noteEn: Dejé is a completed-past form of dejar for “I.” It can say that the speaker left something in the condition described next. Dejar de followed by an action is a different construction meaning to stop that action.

cardUpdates.answerEn: to go down; to become unavailable (a service or system)
cardUpdates.noteEn: Caerse can describe a website, service, or system stopping working. It is not a physical fall in this use. The attached se belongs to this verb use; a changed form is el servicio se cae, “the service goes down.”

example.es: La web puede caerse si hay demasiadas visitas.
example.en: The website can go down if it gets too many visits.

cardUpdates.answerEn: greatest; biggest (plural)
cardUpdates.noteEn: Mayores is the plural of mayor when comparing scale or importance. In a group identified with las or a possessive word such as mis, it can identify the greatest ones. It has the same form for masculine and feminine nouns; the separate age meaning is “older.”

cardUpdates.answerEn: large; big (before a singular noun)
cardUpdates.noteEn: Grande shortens to gran before one masculine or feminine noun. In this size meaning, gran describes a large amount or scale. This is separate from using gran as praise, such as “excellent.”

example.es: Cayó una gran cantidad de nieve.
example.en: A large amount of snow fell.

cardUpdates.answerEn: make; cause (plural)
cardUpdates.noteEn: Hacen is a form of hacer for they or plural you. In this meaning, people or things cause an action or a resulting condition. The words that follow show what happens: hacen reír means “make laugh,” while hacen difícil means “make difficult.”

cardUpdates.answerEn: bad (feminine singular)
some; a bit of
cardUpdates.noteEn: In algo de followed by a noun, algo gives an unspecified amount rather than naming an unspecified thing. Algo stays unchanged; de connects it to what there is some of.

cardUpdates.promptEs: acabar seguido de una acción en -ando o -iendo
cardUpdates.questionEn: How do you use acabar to say that someone ends up doing something?
cardUpdates.answerEn: Use a form of acabar followed by the action in its -ando or -iendo form.
cardUpdates.noteEn: Only acabar changes for the person and time: acaba hablando, acabaron hablando. The second form names the eventual action, which may be unintended. This form is called a gerund: hablar becomes hablando, comer becomes comiendo, and some verbs change their stem, as morir becomes muriendo. Do not add de: acabar de hablar means having just spoken, a different pattern.

example.en: After arguing, we ended up laughing.

cardUpdates.promptEs: es + descripción + verbo en forma de diccionario
cardUpdates.questionEn: How do you use es to say that an activity is easy, difficult, useful, or similar?
cardUpdates.answerEn: Use es, then a describing word, then the activity verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cardUpdates.noteEn: The plus signs mean put the pieces in that order. The dictionary form ends in -ar, -er, or -ir: esperar, aprender, salir. It names the activity in general rather than saying who does it. Spanish needs no separate word for the English it in 'It is difficult to wait.' For a past evaluation, es can change to era or fue; the activity still keeps its dictionary form.

cardUpdates.questionEn: How do you use hacer to say that something makes a person or thing a certain way?
cardUpdates.answerEn: Use hacer with the affected person or thing and a word describing the resulting quality.
cardUpdates.noteEn: The plus signs show the pieces, but a short word for the affected person or thing goes before the changed verb: me hace feliz ('it makes me happy'), los hace fuertes ('it makes them strong'). Hacer changes for what causes the result and for the time: hace, hacen, hizo. The describing word matches what is affected: contento becomes contenta for a woman and contentos for a masculine or mixed group. This pattern describes a quality, not a separate action someone is made to do.

cardUpdates.promptEs: haya, hayas, hayamos, hayáis o hayan + acción completada
cardUpdates.questionEn: How do you use haya hablado and similar forms for an earlier event that is doubted, desired, or evaluated?
cardUpdates.answerEn: Use the matching form of haber—haya, hayas, hayamos, hayáis, or hayan—followed by the verb's completed-action form.
cardUpdates.noteEn: The plus sign means 'followed by.' These haber forms are called subjunctive: they are used when the surrounding words frame an event through doubt, wishes, evaluation, or an unidentified person or thing, rather than simply reporting it. Compare han salido, 'they have left,' with dudo que hayan salido, 'I doubt that they have left.' Haya serves I, he, she, or formal singular you; hayas is familiar singular you, hayamos is we, hayáis is familiar plural you mainly in Spain, and hayan is they or plural you with ustedes. Ustedes is the usual plural you in Latin America and formal plural you in most of Spain. The completed-action form stays unchanged: hablar becomes hablado, comer becomes comido, and hacer becomes hecho.

example.en: I doubt that they have left.

cardUpdates.promptEs: aunque seguido de una situación imaginada en -ra o -se
cardUpdates.questionEn: How do you use aunque to say 'even if' about an imagined or unlikely situation?
cardUpdates.answerEn: Use aunque and a special verb form such as tuviera or tuviese for the imagined condition.
cardUpdates.noteEn: These forms are called the imperfect subjunctive. Here they present a possibility as imagined or remote, not necessarily as an event in the past. An ordinary tiene ('has') becomes tuviera or tuviese ('had' in 'even if she had'); llueve becomes lloviera or lloviese. The main part often uses a would-form such as iría, 'would go.' Aunque can also introduce known facts, but that is a different use.

example.en: Even if it rained, we would go.

cardUpdates.promptEs: verbo en forma de diccionario como etiqueta o instrucción
cardUpdates.questionEn: Why can abrir ('to open') mean 'Open!' on a sign or button?
cardUpdates.answerEn: Spanish can use a verb's dictionary form to label an action or give a short written instruction. English often translates it without 'to.'
cardUpdates.noteEn: The dictionary form is called the infinitive. It ends in -ar, -er, or -ir, as in cerrar ('to close'), comer ('to eat'), and abrir ('to open'). Buttons, signs, diagrams, and written steps can keep it unchanged to name an action without addressing a particular person. When speaking directly to one person informally, a command usually has a different form: abrir becomes abre. The example is a written instruction.

cardUpdates.questionEn: How does alguno or alguna after a noun add 'any at all' to a negative statement?
cardUpdates.answerEn: Put alguno or alguna after the thing that is absent, in a setting made negative by no or sin.
cardUpdates.noteEn: The plus signs show the order of the pieces, but no may be separated from the noun by a verb: no tengo duda alguna. This formal or emphatic order strengthens the absence. Use alguno with a masculine singular noun, such as temor, and alguna with a feminine singular noun, such as duda. After the noun, alguno keeps its final o; it does not shorten to algún.

example.en: I have no doubt at all.

cardUpdates.promptEs: persona o cosa no identificada + que + descripción
cardUpdates.questionEn: How do you choose the verb after que when describing someone or something that has not been identified?
cardUpdates.answerEn: Use the special subjunctive form when you want any suitable person or thing, or are not treating its existence as established.
cardUpdates.noteEn: The plus signs mean name the person or thing, add que ('who' or 'that'), then describe it. Subjunctive is the name for verb forms used here for a wanted or possible description rather than a known example. Compare conozco a alguien que habla inglés, 'I know someone who speaks English,' with busco a alguien que hable inglés, 'I am looking for someone who speaks English.' Habla changes to hable because no particular suitable person is identified. Similar choices occur after cualquier ('any') or when a suitable thing may not exist; the word que alone does not force this form.

example.es: Necesito un libro que explique esto.
example.en: I need a book that explains this.

cardUpdates.promptEs: se + poder + acción en forma de diccionario
cardUpdates.questionEn: How do you use se and poder to say that something can be done without naming who does it?
cardUpdates.answerEn: Use se, a form of poder, and the action's dictionary form; se can instead attach to the end of that action.
cardUpdates.noteEn: The plus signs mean put the pieces in order. The dictionary form ends in -ar, -er, or -ir and stays unchanged. When wording focuses on things receiving an action, poder matches them: la puerta se puede abrir, but las puertas se pueden abrir. The same order can be las puertas pueden abrirse. Other settings change puede to forms such as podía or pueda. Do not assume every se sentence has this agreement. Se puede caminar ('one can walk') talks about people acting in general, without a thing receiving the action to make poder plural, so use singular puede.

example.es: Las entradas pueden comprarse en línea.
example.en: The tickets can be bought online.

cardUpdates.questionEn: How do you use tardar en to say how long someone takes to do something?
cardUpdates.answerEn: Use a form of tardar, optionally state the time taken, then en and the action in its dictionary form.
cardUpdates.noteEn: The plus signs show the order of the pieces; 'tiempo opcional' means the time amount can be omitted. Tardar changes for who takes the time and when: tardo, tardan, tardaron. The final verb keeps its -ar, -er, or -ir dictionary form: tardan en llegar. Keep en even though English usually has no separate word for it. You can state a duration, use mucho ('a long time'), or ask cuánto ('how long').

example.en: They took two hours to arrive.

cardUpdates.promptEs: me, te, le, nos, os o les + gusta + actividad
cardUpdates.questionEn: How do you use gusta to say that someone likes doing an activity?
cardUpdates.answerEn: Choose the short word for the person, add gusta, then name the activity with the verb's dictionary form.
cardUpdates.noteEn: The plus signs mean put the pieces in that order. Use me for me, te for familiar singular you, le for him/her/formal singular you, nos for us, os for familiar plural you mainly in Spain, and les for them or plural you with ustedes. Ustedes is the usual plural you in Latin America and formal plural you in most of Spain. The activity is what pleases that person, so gusta stays singular for one activity even with les. Its action verb keeps its -ar, -er, or -ir dictionary form. To name or emphasize the people, add a before their name or group: a mis amigos les gusta leer. No before the short word makes it negative.

example.es: A mis vecinos les gusta cocinar.

cardUpdates.promptEs: orden afirmativa con una palabra corta al final
cardUpdates.questionEn: Where do te ('yourself'), lo ('it'), and similar short words go with a command to do something?
cardUpdates.answerEn: Attach them to the end of an affirmative command and write the result as one word.
cardUpdates.noteEn: An affirmative command tells someone to do something, rather than not to do it. This attachment works with both familiar and formal commands: sienta and te form siéntate; envíe and lo form envíelo. The short words stand for a person or thing involved in the action; they are called pronouns. A written accent may be needed to preserve the command's original stress. With a negative command, put these words before the verb instead: no te sientes. Choosing the correct command ending is a separate step.

cardUpdates.promptEs: parar de + acción en forma de diccionario
cardUpdates.questionEn: How do you use parar de to say that someone stops doing an action?
cardUpdates.answerEn: Use a form of parar, then de, then the action verb in its dictionary form.
cardUpdates.noteEn: The plus sign means 'followed by.' The dictionary form is the unchanged verb ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. Only parar changes for the person and time: paro de hablar, paras de hablar, pararon de hablar. Keep de even though English does not translate it separately. Adding no makes the person not stop, often expressed in English as 'keep doing': no para de hablar. This is different from pararse a hablar, which means stopping in order to talk.

cardUpdates.promptEs: acción en -ando o -iendo con me, te, se, nos u os al final
cardUpdates.questionEn: How do you attach me, te, se, nos, or os to an action form such as preparando?
cardUpdates.answerEn: Join the matching short word to the end of the -ando or -iendo form, adding an accent when needed to keep the original stress.
cardUpdates.noteEn: Some verbs are learned with se, such as lavarse ('wash oneself') or prepararse ('get ready'). Choose me for I, te for familiar singular you, se for he/she/formal you or they, nos for we, and os for familiar plural you mainly in Spain. The marker may describe an action done to oneself, or be part of the verb's meaning without a separate English 'self.' An -ando or -iendo action form is called a gerund: preparando and me become preparándome; lavando and se become lavándose. This card teaches the attachment, not a different sense for every verb.

example.en: I am getting ready to leave.

cardUpdates.questionEn: After es importante que or es mejor que, how do you express the action being judged?
cardUpdates.answerEn: Use a form of ser, the evaluation, que, and the action in its special subjunctive form.
cardUpdates.noteEn: The plus signs show the pieces in order. Subjunctive is the name for the verb form used here because the action is being evaluated, not simply reported. Compare descansas ('you rest') with es importante que descanses ('it is important that you rest'): descansas changes to descanses. Ser can change for time, as in será mejor que llegues. This applies to judgments such as bueno, importante, raro, or mejor, not every adjective: es cierto que presents something as true and normally uses an ordinary statement form. For an activity in general without a separate person, use es importante descansar, with no que.

example.en: It is better for you to rest.

cardUpdates.questionEn: How do you use algo de to mean 'some' or 'a bit of' a thing or substance?
cardUpdates.answerEn: Put algo de before the thing whose amount you leave unspecified.
cardUpdates.noteEn: The plus sign means 'followed by.' Algo alone means 'something'; algo de before a noun means an unspecified amount of it. Both algo and de stay unchanged: algo de agua, algo de tiempo, algo de ayuda. The name after de tells you what the amount consists of. This is especially useful for substances, time, help, and other things treated as amounts rather than counted individuals.

cardUpdates.promptEs: llamar a una persona o cosa por un nombre
cardUpdates.questionEn: How do you use llamar to say what name or label someone gives a person or thing?
cardUpdates.answerEn: Use a form of llamar with the person or thing being named and the name or label.
cardUpdates.noteEn: Here llamar means 'call by a name,' not 'telephone.' The order can vary: llamamos Nena a Elena puts the label first, while a Elena la llaman Nena names the person first and repeats her with la. A short word such as lo, la, or—in common Spanish usage for a male person—le can represent the person. Llamar changes for who uses the name and for the time: llamamos, llamaban. The same naming pattern can label things: llamamos refugio a este lugar.

cardUpdates.questionEn: How do you say 'I'm sorry' or 'we're sorry' with lo siento?
cardUpdates.answerEn: Use lo siento when speaking for yourself and lo sentimos when speaking for a group.
cardUpdates.noteEn: Use this conventional expression for an apology or for sympathy about bad news. Lo stays fixed, while sentir changes to siento for I and sentimos for we. Mucho can strengthen the apology: lo siento mucho. These are variations of the same expression, not separate meanings of apology.

example.en: We're sorry. It was a mistake.

cardUpdates.questionEn: How do you use luchar por to say what someone fights for or strives to achieve?
cardUpdates.answerEn: Use a form of luchar, then por, then the cause, person, or goal the effort supports.
cardUpdates.noteEn: The plus sign means 'followed by.' Luchar changes for the person and time: lucho, luchan, luchamos. Por stays fixed. A noun can name the cause, as in luchar por la libertad. If the goal is an action, leave that action in its -ar, -er, or -ir dictionary form: luchar por mejorar. The effort may be literal fighting or determined work toward a goal.

example.en: We strive to improve our conditions.

cardUpdates.promptEs: se trata de + asunto o acción
cardUpdates.questionEn: How do you use se trata de to introduce what something involves or what the point is?
cardUpdates.answerEn: Use se trata de before the matter involved, or before an action in its dictionary form.
cardUpdates.noteEn: The plus sign means 'followed by.' This expression has no named person or thing doing the verb; this is called an impersonal expression. Keep the verb singular even before plural things: se trata de dos problemas. It can change for time, as in se trataba de. An action keeps its -ar, -er, or -ir dictionary form. Ask ¿de qué se trata? when the matter is unknown. Do not add a subject such as la película to se trata de; a named film uses la película trata de without se.

example.es: Se trata de aprender, no de ganar.
example.en: The point is to learn, not to win.

cardUpdates.questionEn: How do you use hace to say how long ago something happened?
cardUpdates.answerEn: Put hace before the amount of time between now and the past event.
cardUpdates.noteEn: The plus sign means 'followed by.' Hace stays singular and comes before the duration: hace dos años means 'two years ago.' The amount can be vague: hace un tiempo means 'a while ago,' and hace mucho means 'a long time ago.' The event itself is normally expressed in a past form. This card covers when a past event happened, not the different pattern hace dos años que vivo aquí for something continuing until now.

cardUpdates.questionEn: How do you use lo to mean 'the good part,' 'what is important,' or another general quality?
cardUpdates.answerEn: Put lo before the masculine singular form of a describing word, without adding a noun.
cardUpdates.noteEn: The plus sign means 'followed by.' A describing word is called an adjective: bueno means good and difícil means difficult. Lo turns that quality into a general thing or aspect, as in lo bueno ('the good part') and lo difícil ('what is difficult'). It does not refer to a masculine object. Keep the describing word masculine singular: lo bueno, not lo buena or lo buenos. Lo mejor likewise means the best thing or part; mejor itself supplies 'best.'

cardUpdates.questionEn: How do you use hacerse to say that someone or something becomes a certain way?
cardUpdates.answerEn: Use the matching form of hacerse followed by the word describing the new state.
cardUpdates.noteEn: The plus sign means 'followed by.' The short marker and hacer change together: me hago ('I become'), te haces ('you become,' familiar singular), se hace ('he/she becomes'), nos hacemos ('we become'). This often describes development or a change over time, including getting older: hacerse mayor. The describing word matches the person or thing when its ending allows it: mayor becomes mayores for a group; rico becomes rica for a woman. Not every English 'become' uses hacerse: sudden temporary feelings and changes of identity can use other Spanish verbs.

example.es: Las tardes se hacen más cortas.

cardUpdates.questionEn: How do you use ser capaz de to say that someone is able to do something?
cardUpdates.answerEn: Use a form of ser, then capaz de, then the action verb in its dictionary form.
cardUpdates.noteEn: The plus sign means 'followed by.' The dictionary form ends in -ar, -er, or -ir and stays unchanged. Ser changes for the person and time, and capaz becomes capaces for more than one person. Keep de when stating the action: somos capaces de nadar. The action can be left out when it is already clear. No before ser makes it negative; context can turn 'you are not capable' into a challenge about what someone would dare do.

cardUpdates.promptEs: por aquí, por ahí o por allí
cardUpdates.questionEn: How do por aquí, por ahí, and por allí point to an approximate area or route?
cardUpdates.answerEn: Put por before aquí, ahí, or allí to mean around here, around there, or this/that way.
cardUpdates.noteEn: Por makes the place or route approximate rather than a single exact point. Aquí points near the speaker, ahí generally points away from the speaker, and allí points farther away. The words stay unchanged. With movement, por ahí can also mean being out and about rather than going to a precise named destination.

cardUpdates.questionEn: How do you add 'or something' or 'or something like that' to an informal suggestion?
cardUpdates.answerEn: Add o algo after the suggestion; add así if you mean 'or something like that.'
cardUpdates.noteEn: These words stay unchanged. O algo leaves the alternative open rather than insisting on one exact thing. Optional así points to something similar to what you just mentioned. The phrase can soften a suggestion or mark a description or estimate as approximate; it does not make the preceding statement exact.

example.es: Podemos tomar un café o algo.
example.en: We can have a coffee or something.

cardUpdates.promptEs: importar con la persona a quien le importa
cardUpdates.questionEn: How do you use importar to say what matters and who cares about it?
cardUpdates.answerEn: Make importar match the thing or person that matters; use me, te, le, nos, os, or les to say who cares.
cardUpdates.noteEn: For one thing or a whole situation, use importa; for several things, use importan: me importa el precio, me importan los detalles. The short word names who cares: me is to me, te to familiar singular you, le to him/her/formal singular you, nos to us, os to familiar plural you mainly in Spain, and les to them or plural you with ustedes. Ustedes is the usual plural you in Latin America and formal plural you in most of Spain. If I am the person who matters, use importo, as in le importo ('I matter to him or her'). You can omit the person when it is not needed: importa el resultado. No makes it negative and goes before the short word, if present: no me importa.

cardUpdates.questionEn: How do you use quedarse to say that someone remains in or ends up in a state?
cardUpdates.answerEn: Use a matching form of quedarse, then the word or phrase naming the continuing or resulting state.
cardUpdates.noteEn: The plus sign means 'followed by.' Change the short marker and quedar for the person and time: me quedo ('I stay'), te quedas ('you stay,' familiar singular), se quedó ('he/she stayed'), nos quedamos ('we stay' or 'we stayed'). The marker is part of this verb even when English has no separate word for it. A describing word matches the person: callado becomes callada for a woman and callados for a masculine or mixed group. Other state words, such as fuera ('outside'), stay unchanged. Context tells you whether the state continues or is a new result.

cardUpdates.questionEn: How do you use suficiente para to say that an amount is enough to do something?
cardUpdates.answerEn: Describe the amount with suficiente, then use para and the action verb in its dictionary form.
cardUpdates.noteEn: The plus signs show the pieces in order. Suficiente can come before or after the noun: suficiente comida or comida suficiente. It becomes suficientes with a plural noun, as in suficientes personas. The action after para keeps its -ar, -er, or -ir dictionary form. This describes the result the amount makes possible, including enough time, food, money, or age; the surrounding verb is not part of the fixed pattern.

example.es: Hay comida suficiente para alimentar a todos.
example.en: There is enough food to feed everyone.

cardUpdates.promptEs: hacer + persona + acción en forma de diccionario
cardUpdates.questionEn: How do you use hacer with a dictionary-form verb to say that something makes someone act?
cardUpdates.answerEn: Use a form of hacer and the action in its dictionary form, with a word identifying who is made to act.
cardUpdates.noteEn: The plus signs show the pieces, not a fixed position for the person word. The dictionary form ends in -ar, -er, or -ir and stays unchanged. Hacer changes for what causes the action and when it happens: hace, hacen, hizo. Short affected-person words such as me, te, or nos go before the changed verb: me hace reír. If hacer uses the helper haber, put the short word before that helper: nos ha hecho reír. This card is about causing an action, not making someone have a quality such as feliz.

cardUpdates.promptEs: pensar en + persona, cosa o idea
cardUpdates.questionEn: How do you use pensar en to say what someone is thinking about?
cardUpdates.answerEn: Use a form of pensar, then en, then the person, thing, or idea that comes to mind.
cardUpdates.noteEn: The plus sign means 'followed by.' Pensar changes for the person and time: pienso, pensamos, pensaron. En stays in place before what comes to mind. Depending on context, English uses 'think of' or 'think about.' Do not omit en in this pattern; pensar followed directly by a dictionary-form verb can instead express an intention.

example.en: I am thinking about my friends.

cardUpdates.questionEn: When do you reply a mí también to mean 'me too'?
cardUpdates.answerEn: Use a mí también when the same experience or feeling applies to you in a pattern such as me gusta or me pasa.
cardUpdates.noteEn: Mí is the emphasized form of 'me' after a and needs its accent. Keep a because you are the person to whom something is pleasing or happening: me gusta el jazz → a mí también. This is not the reply for every English 'me too.' When you are simply doing the same action, use yo también: trabajo aquí → yo también. También is for an affirmative agreement; a negative agreement uses tampoco.

cardUpdates.promptEs: el mes, la semana o el año que viene
cardUpdates.questionEn: How do you use que viene to say 'next week,' 'next month,' or 'next year'?
cardUpdates.answerEn: Name the time period with el or la, then add que viene.
cardUpdates.noteEn: Que viene means 'that is coming.' Use la semana que viene, el mes que viene, or el año que viene. El or la matches the time word; viene stays singular because each example describes one coming period. The expression names the next such period, not an arbitrary future one.

example.en: We are coming back next week.

cardUpdates.questionEn: How do you use estar convencido de que to say what someone is convinced is true?
cardUpdates.answerEn: Use the matching form of estar and convencido, then de que and the belief.
cardUpdates.noteEn: The plus sign means put the belief after de que. Estar changes for the person and time: estoy, está, estaban. Convencido also matches the person: convencida for a woman, convencidos for a masculine or mixed group, and convencidas for a female group. Keep de before que: convencido de names what someone is convinced of, and que introduces a statement about it. This affirmative pattern presents that statement as the person's belief.

example.en: We are convinced that it will work.

cardUpdates.promptEs: el mes pasado, la semana pasada o el año pasado
cardUpdates.questionEn: How do you use pasado or pasada to say 'last week,' 'last month,' or 'last year'?
cardUpdates.answerEn: Name the time period with el or la, then add pasado or pasada to mean the most recent completed one.
cardUpdates.noteEn: Use la semana pasada, el mes pasado, or el año pasado. The describing word follows the time word and matches it: semana is feminine, so use pasada; mes and año are masculine, so use pasado. This names the preceding calendar period, not merely any time in the past.

cardUpdates.questionEn: How do you say 'step by step' or 'day by day' by repeating a Spanish word?
cardUpdates.answerEn: Repeat the singular unit with a between the two copies: paso a paso, día a día, minuto a minuto.
cardUpdates.noteEn: The plus signs show the order; 'la misma unidad' means repeat exactly the same unit. This pattern describes gradual progress or attention to each successive unit. Both copies normally stay singular and have no el or la in front. The unit can be time, as in día a día, or a step in a process, as in paso a paso.

example.es: Resolvimos el problema paso a paso.
example.en: We solved the problem step by step.

cardUpdates.questionEn: How do you say that a drawing or model is 'to scale' in Spanish?
cardUpdates.answerEn: Use a escala when its sizes follow the same proportion as the real object.
cardUpdates.noteEn: A escala is a fixed expression: a and escala stay unchanged. It describes proportional sizes, not necessarily a life-size image. Adding no gives 'not to scale,' but the useful unit is a escala. A drawing marked no a escala should not be used to infer true relative sizes or distances.

cardUpdates.promptEs: ponérselo fácil o difícil a alguien
cardUpdates.questionEn: How do you use poner with lo to say that someone makes things easy or difficult for another person?
cardUpdates.answerEn: Use a short word for the affected person, lo, a form of poner, then fácil or difícil.
cardUpdates.noteEn: Lo stands for the situation. The person word comes first: me lo pones fácil ('you make it easy for me'), nos lo ponen difícil ('they make it difficult for us'). Use me, te, nos, or os as needed; le and les change to se immediately before lo, giving se lo, not le lo or les lo. Poner changes for who causes the situation and for the time: pones, puso; with haber, its completed-action form is puesto, as in me lo has puesto fácil. Fácil and difícil describe the difficulty of the situation, not the person's gender.

example.en: They made it difficult for us.

cardUpdates.promptEs: ¿Qué te, le, os o les parece?
cardUpdates.questionEn: How do you use ¿qué te parece? and similar questions to ask someone's opinion?
cardUpdates.answerEn: Ask ¿qué te parece…? with a familiar listener, changing te to le, os, or les for the person or people whose opinion you want.
cardUpdates.noteEn: Parecer means 'seem': the question asks how something seems to someone. Te is familiar singular you; le is him, her, or formal singular you; os is familiar plural you mainly in Spain; les is them or plural you with ustedes. Ustedes is the usual plural you in Latin America and formal plural you in most of Spain. The thing being judged controls parece or parecen: ¿qué te parecen estas ideas? uses plural parecen for ideas. The three dots leave a place for what you are asking about.

example.en: What do you think of this plan?

cardUpdates.promptEs: en rojo, en verde o en ámbar
cardUpdates.questionEn: How do you use en and a color to describe a traffic signal's current state?
cardUpdates.answerEn: Put en before the color the signal is showing: en rojo, en verde, or en ámbar.
cardUpdates.noteEn: This describes the signal's current operating state, not the paint color of the object. The expression stays unchanged even with several signals: semáforos en rojo. You can name the signal before it or use estar, as in el semáforo está en verde. Rojo is one current state, not a different language pattern from verde or ámbar.

cardUpdates.questionEn: How do you use lejos de to say that something is far from a place or reference point?
cardUpdates.answerEn: Use lejos de followed by the place or reference point.
cardUpdates.noteEn: The plus sign means 'followed by.' Lejos de stays unchanged: lejos de casa, lejos del centro. Del combines de and el when the reference point starts with el. A word such as muy ('very') or tan ('so') can intensify the distance, but it is optional and not part of the fixed unit.

example.en: We live far from the center.

cardUpdates.promptEs: todo un o toda una + nombre
cardUpdates.questionEn: How do todo un and toda una add the sense of 'a whole' or 'quite a' before a noun?
cardUpdates.answerEn: Put todo un before a masculine noun or toda una before a feminine noun to emphasize its size, importance, or full character.
cardUpdates.noteEn: The plus sign means 'followed by.' Match both words to the noun: todo un reto ('quite a challenge'), toda una aventura ('a real adventure'). This is an emphatic way to present one thing, not a count of many things. Context decides whether natural English says 'a whole,' 'quite a,' or 'a real.' The noun is a replaceable example, not part of a separate expression.

example.es: El viaje fue toda una aventura.
example.en: The trip was quite an adventure.

cardUpdates.answerEn: at; introduces a measured distance, speed, or rate
cardUpdates.noteEn: A can connect an action or situation to its measured distance or rate. The number and unit tell you what is being measured; a itself does not change.

example.es: El tren viaja a cien kilómetros por hora.
example.en: The train travels at one hundred kilometres per hour.

cardUpdates.answerEn: to; introduces the endpoint of a connection
cardUpdates.noteEn: Use a after conectar or conectarse to name what the connection reaches. The connecting verb can change for the person and time, but a stays the same.

example.es: Conecta el cable a la batería.
example.en: Connect the cable to the battery.

cardUpdates.answerEn: no separate English word; marks a person or animate target directly acted on
cardUpdates.noteEn: Spanish usually puts a before a known person directly affected by a verb, and before person words such as alguien or nadie. Animals and things treated as person-like can also take it. This does not mean movement 'to' someone or giving something to a recipient.

example.es: Veo a Marta, pero no veo a su perro.
example.en: I see Marta, but I do not see her dog.

cardUpdates.answerEn: to; introduces the test, condition, or constraint something is subject to
cardUpdates.noteEn: With someter and forms such as sometido or sometida, a introduces the condition applied to someone or something. The verb or description may change, but this a stays unchanged.

example.es: Sometieron el motor a varias pruebas.
example.en: They subjected the engine to several tests.

cardUpdates.answerEn: to; introduces what time, effort, or activity is devoted to
cardUpdates.noteEn: Dedicar and dedicarse use a before the recipient, field, or activity receiving someone's time or effort. An action after a stays in its dictionary form, such as estudiar, 'to study.'

example.en: I devote an hour to studying.

cardUpdates.answerEn: no separate English word; links parar to the action that stops
cardUpdates.noteEn: Keep de between a form of parar and an action in its dictionary form: the unchanged form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. Parar changes for the person and time; de and the next action form do not.

cardUpdates.answerEn: often no separate English word; links a noun to its type, purpose, or field
cardUpdates.noteEn: Spanish often puts de between two nouns where English puts the describing noun first. In una silla de oficina, oficina tells you the chair's intended use. This is different from de naming an owner, material, contents, or a part's larger whole.

cardUpdates.answerEn: of; identifies the larger group or whole
cardUpdates.noteEn: De links a selected amount or member to the group it comes from, as in uno de, algunos de, or la mayoría de. It also appears with nada de when none of the stated whole is included. De itself does not change.

example.es: Algunos de mis amigos viven aquí.
example.en: Some of my friends live here.

cardUpdates.answerEn: no separate English word; links antes to what happens later
cardUpdates.noteEn: Antes de means 'before.' De stays after antes before a noun, an action's dictionary form, or que followed by an event. The dictionary form is the unchanged verb ending in -ar, -er, or -ir, such as salir.

cardUpdates.answerEn: no separate English word; links es hora to what it is time for
cardUpdates.noteEn: After es hora, keep de before the activity. An action can follow in its dictionary form, as in salir, or de que can introduce who should act and a changed verb form. De belongs to the link in both versions.

cardUpdates.answerEn: no separate English word; links tardar to the action taking time
cardUpdates.noteEn: Tardar uses en before the action that takes time. That action stays in its dictionary form, such as llegar, 'to arrive.' A duration can appear between tardar and en; only tardar changes for the person and time.

example.en: I took ten minutes to arrive.

cardUpdates.answerEn: in; introduces what someone is interested in
cardUpdates.noteEn: Use en with interesarse or interesado to name the interest. Interesado can change to interesada, interesados, or interesadas to match the person or people; en does not change.

example.es: Clara está interesada en la música.

cardUpdates.answerEn: in; introduces who or what is trusted
cardUpdates.noteEn: Confiar and confianza use en before the person, thing, or ability being trusted. Keep en even when natural English chooses a verb such as 'trust' without a separate 'in.'

cardUpdates.answerEn: into; introduces what something becomes
cardUpdates.noteEn: With a change verb such as convertirse or degenerar, en introduces the resulting thing or situation. The verb supplies the kind of change; en itself does not mean that the result is good or bad.

example.es: El agua se convierte en hielo.

cardUpdates.answerEn: no separate English word; focuses on what receives an action, without naming the doer
cardUpdates.noteEn: Se can present the thing acted on without naming who acts. The verb normally matches that thing: se vende una casa, but se venden dos casas. English often uses 'is' or 'are' plus a form such as 'sold.' Adding poder expresses possibility without changing se's role.

cardUpdates.answerEn: no separate English word; presents something as undergoing a change
cardUpdates.noteEn: With some verbs, se makes the named thing the one that changes, rather than the thing someone changes. Compare Marta abre la puerta with la puerta se abre. The verb still changes for the thing and time; se does not say that it deliberately acts on itself.

cardUpdates.answerEn: no separate English word; can emphasize doing an action through or completely
cardUpdates.noteEn: With actions such as comer or leer, se can emphasize doing the action over a specified thing, as in eating something up or reading it through. It does not mean 'himself' here. Se goes with él, ella, usted, ellos, ellas, or ustedes; other people use matching words such as me or te.

cardUpdates.answerEn: per; for each
cardUpdates.noteEn: Por introduces the unit across which a quantity is distributed. The unit can be a person, item, or stretch of time. Por does not change, and a single-unit expression normally names the unit in the singular.

example.en: There are two books per student.

cardUpdates.answerEn: because of; for a reason
cardUpdates.noteEn: Por can introduce the cause or reason for something, before a noun or an action in its dictionary form. It explains why something happens, not the goal someone wants to achieve.

example.es: Cerraron la calle por la nieve.
example.en: They closed the street because of the snow.

cardUpdates.answerEn: that; links an expression to its content or an outcome
cardUpdates.noteEn: Que can introduce what someone thinks, says, wants, causes, or allows, or what an evaluation is about. English may use 'that,' omit it, or reorganize the sentence with 'to' or 'for.' Que stays unaccented; the following verb form depends on the surrounding expression.

example.en: I think that Ana is coming.

cardUpdates.answerEn: at; for; introduces the field of a skill or talent
cardUpdates.noteEn: After bueno, malo, don, or talento, para names the activity or field in which someone has or lacks ability. Para stays the same even when the other words change.

example.en: She has a talent for music.

cardUpdates.answerEn: for; introduces an intended recipient, user, or audience
cardUpdates.noteEn: Para can identify who something is meant for, including a person, animal, or device. This differs from para before an action naming a purpose, and from describing the conditions something is suitable for.

cardUpdates.answerEn: the; a + el before a person or animate target directly acted on
cardUpdates.noteEn: Al combines a and el. This a marks a person, animal, or person-like target directly affected by the verb; it does not itself mean 'to' a recipient. El means 'the,' or helps identify 'the one' when no noun is stated. Keep al separate from accented él, 'he.'

cardUpdates.answerEn: marks me as the person who feels, likes, or experiences something
cardUpdates.noteEn: Me identifies the speaker as the person having a feeling, impression, preference, or difficulty. English often makes this person 'I,' while Spanish builds its wording around what produces the reaction. Compare me gusta el libro with me gustan los libros: me stays the same.

cardUpdates.answerEn: marks me as the person whose body, possessions, or situation is affected
cardUpdates.noteEn: Spanish can use me for the affected owner and el or la before the thing involved. English often says 'my' or 'from me' instead. Me identifies the person; the article before the thing matches that thing, not its owner.

cardUpdates.answerEn: with
cardUpdates.noteEn: Con introduces someone or something accompanying, involved in, or used for an action. It does not change for the person or time. Some verbs require it, as in hablar con alguien, 'to talk with someone.'

cardUpdates.answerEn: to; with; connects related things
cardUpdates.noteEn: Relación and relacionado use con to introduce what something is connected or related to. Relacionado may change to relacionada, relacionados, or relacionadas; con stays unchanged. English commonly uses 'to' in 'related to.'

example.es: El cambio no tiene relación con el precio.
example.en: The change is not related to the price.

cardUpdates.answerEn: from the; identifies the time or period something comes from
cardUpdates.noteEn: Del is the required combination of de and el. In this use, de gives a time of origin or a period something belongs to, rather than an owner. The expression may name a century, season, year, or the past or future.

example.en: It is a letter from the past.

cardUpdates.answerEn: marks one person or entity as the one having a feeling, preference, or impression
cardUpdates.noteEn: Le can identify him, her, formal you, or another singular person or entity experiencing a reaction. What causes the reaction controls the verb: le gusta el libro, but le gustan los libros. Le stays the same; a phrase such as a Ana can clarify who it refers to.

example.es: A Ana le gustan los trenes.

cardUpdates.answerEn: marks one person or entity affected by what happens
cardUpdates.noteEn: Le can identify the person whose body, possessions, or situation is affected, even when nothing is literally given to them. It can refer to him, her, or formal you. English may use 'his,' 'her,' 'your,' or 'to' or 'with' that person; the surrounding words identify who is meant.

example.es: Le lavé las manos al niño.

cardUpdates.answerEn: the; English often uses my, your, or another owner's word
cardUpdates.noteEn: Spanish often uses la before a feminine singular body part or close possession when me, te, le, or the surrounding context already identifies the affected owner. La matches the thing, not the owner's gender. It does not itself specify whose it is.

cardUpdates.answerEn: her; it; formal you, for one woman
cardUpdates.noteEn: La can replace a woman or a thing whose Spanish name is feminine when it directly receives an action. It can also address one woman formally as usted. It usually comes before a changed verb; it does not mean the article 'the' in this use.

example.es: Tengo una carta y la leo.
example.en: I have a letter and I am reading it.

cardUpdates.answerEn: no separate English word; accompanies a verb used with tú
cardUpdates.noteEn: Some verbs conventionally use a matching small word: me with 'I,' te with one familiar 'you,' and se with 'he,' 'she,' or formal 'you.' Te is part of that verb's use even when nobody literally acts on themselves. Its contribution often has no separate English translation.

cardUpdates.answerEn: to you; for you, as the recipient
cardUpdates.noteEn: Te can identify one familiar listener as the person receiving something or benefiting from an action. It normally goes before the verb. English may say 'to you' or 'for you,' or simply place 'you' before what is given or said.

cardUpdates.answerEn: marks you as the person who feels, likes, or experiences something
cardUpdates.noteEn: Te identifies one familiar listener as the person having a feeling, impression, or preference. English often starts with 'you,' while Spanish builds the sentence around what produces the reaction: te gusta el libro, but te gustan los libros. Te stays the same.

cardUpdates.answerEn: it; that, as the thing or idea acted on
cardUpdates.noteEn: Lo can replace a masculine singular thing or a whole idea that receives an action. It usually comes before the verb and does not name who performs the action. English often uses 'it' or 'that'; with todo, lo can refer to everything being acted on.

example.es: Tengo el libro y lo leo.
example.en: I have the book and I am reading it.

cardUpdates.answerEn: more
cardUpdates.noteEn: Más can describe a greater amount or degree, or stand alone when the missing person or thing is clear. It keeps its written accent; mas without an accent is a different, literary word meaning 'but.'

cardUpdates.answerEn: anymore; no longer, with a negative expression
cardUpdates.noteEn: Ya with a negative expression marks a change from what was true before. Ya no means 'no longer'; with ni siquiera, the sense is 'not even ... anymore.' Ya itself stays unchanged.

cardUpdates.answerEn: already; by now, often yet in a question
cardUpdates.noteEn: Ya marks that an expected action or state has been reached by the time being discussed. English usually says 'already' in a statement, but often 'yet' in a question about whether it has happened.

cardUpdates.answerEn: the; often omitted in English before a named item
cardUpdates.noteEn: Spanish can use el before the name or number of a masculine item, product, command, system, or service. An ordinary noun such as modelo or número may be understood rather than written. English often uses the name alone. El here is not accented él, 'he.'

cardUpdates.answerEn: the; English often uses my, your, or another owner's word
cardUpdates.noteEn: Spanish often uses el before a masculine singular body part or close possession when me, te, le, or the surrounding context already identifies the affected owner. El matches the thing, not its owner's gender; it does not itself say whose it is.

cardUpdates.answerEn: the one; replaces an understood masculine singular noun
cardUpdates.noteEn: El can remain when an already understood masculine noun is left out. The following words identify which one, for example de color azul or que llegó primero. English often supplies 'the one.' Do not confuse this unaccented el with él, 'he.'

cardUpdates.answerEn: as; introduces a role, label, or assigned category
cardUpdates.noteEn: Unaccented como can identify the capacity in which someone acts, what a thing is used as, or the name or category assigned to it. This differs from comparing how similar things are, and from accented cómo, which asks 'how.'

cardUpdates.answerEn: the; English often uses my, your, our, or another owner's word
cardUpdates.noteEn: Spanish often uses los before masculine plural body parts or clothing when the verb, a word such as me or te, or the context already identifies the owner or wearer. Los matches the plural things, not the people they belong to.

cardUpdates.answerEn: the ones; the people, with an understood noun
cardUpdates.noteEn: Los can stand for an unstated masculine or mixed plural group. Words after it identify which group: los de la oficina or los que llegaron. English often supplies 'the people,' 'the ones,' or 'those.'

example.es: Los de la oficina ya llegaron.
example.en: The people from the office have already arrived.

cardUpdates.answerEn: what; which
cardUpdates.noteEn: Qué asks for an unknown thing, action, or choice. It can stand alone, come before a noun, or occur inside a larger statement such as no sé qué elegir. It keeps the written accent even without question marks; que without an accent has other linking uses.

example.en: I do not know which route to choose.

cardUpdates.answerEn: how; part of qué tal
cardUpdates.noteEn: Qué tal asks for an opinion, how someone or something is doing, or how an experience went. It can also suggest an option: 'How about ...?' Qué keeps its accent, and the two words work together.

cardUpdates.answerEn: but; introduces an emphatic objection or reminder
cardUpdates.noteEn: Unaccented si can point to a fact the listener is overlooking, sometimes after pero. In this use it does not mean a conditional 'if,' and it is not accented sí, 'yes.' English may express the objection with 'but' or emphasis.

cardUpdates.answerEn: no separate English word; part of por si, in case
cardUpdates.noteEn: Por si introduces a possibility someone is preparing for. Acaso can be added for 'just in case,' including on its own at the end. Si stays unaccented; it is not sí, 'yes.'

example.es: Lleva una chaqueta por si hace frío.
example.en: Take a jacket in case it is cold.

cardUpdates.answerEn: if
cardUpdates.noteEn: Unaccented si introduces a condition or possibility. With an opening y in a question, ¿y si...? invites someone to consider 'what if ...?' This differs from accented sí, 'yes.'

cardUpdates.answerEn: his; her; its; their; your, with usted or ustedes
cardUpdates.noteEn: Su comes before one possessed thing. It does not show the owner's gender or number: context tells you whose it is. Use sus when the possessed things are plural, even if there is only one owner: su libro, but sus libros. Formal usted and plural ustedes also use su for 'your.'

example.es: Ana abre su libro; los niños abren su caja.
example.en: Ana opens her book; the children open their box.

cardUpdates.answerEn: is; are (formal singular you)
cardUpdates.noteEn: Es is a present form of ser for one person or thing, including usted, the formal way to address one person as 'you.' It can identify, classify, describe, evaluate, or state a time. Spanish can leave the person or thing understood, where English supplies 'he,' 'she,' or 'it.' Compare es with eres for familiar 'you' and son for several people or things.

cardUpdates.answerEn: line; communications connection
to the; introduces the recipient
cardUpdates.noteEn: Al combines a and el. In this use, a introduces who receives something or benefits from an action, rather than the person directly acted on. Before que, el can stand for 'the one.'

example.es: Le entregué la carta al profesor.
example.en: I handed the letter to the teacher.

cardUpdates.answerEn: of; filled with or containing
cardUpdates.noteEn: De can connect a container, area, food, or supply to what it contains. It names the contents or ingredients, not the container's material or its owner. English may use 'of' or put the content word first.

example.en: She brought a bag of sweets.

cardUpdates.answerEn: for; from someone's point of view
cardUpdates.noteEn: Para can introduce the person whose opinion or experience is being described. It does not identify an intended recipient in this use.

example.es: Para Ana, la música es importante.

cardUpdates.answerEn: to you; identifies the person something happens to
cardUpdates.noteEn: Te can identify one familiar listener as the person affected by an event or situation, even when nothing is given to them. With pasar it marks who something happens to; with quedar it can identify who has something remaining.

cardUpdates.answerEn: me; the person allowed to act
cardUpdates.noteEn: Before a form of dejar meaning 'let' or 'allow,' me can identify the speaker as the person receiving permission. The following action stays in its dictionary form, such as entrar, 'to enter.' This differs from me belonging to a following verb that conventionally uses it.

cardUpdates.answerEn: is; part of es que, an explanation opener
cardUpdates.noteEn: Es que is a conversational lead-in used to give a reason, correction, or excuse. English may say 'it's that' or 'the thing is.' This is different from ordinary es after a stated subject, as in el problema es que...

example.es: No salgo; es que estoy cansada.
example.en: I am not going out; the thing is, I am tired.

cardUpdates.answerEn: part of es que, an explanation opener
cardUpdates.noteEn: Que joins es in the conversational expression es que, used to introduce a reason, correction, or excuse. English often reorganizes the expression as 'the thing is.' Que stays unaccented; ordinary que after el problema es... instead introduces what the problem is.

example.en: The thing is, I do not have time.

cardUpdates.promptEs: compresión de audio y tasa de bits
cardUpdates.questionEn: Why can an audio connection lose detail even when the speakers are excellent?
cardUpdates.answerEn: Lossy audio compression saves data by discarding some sound information; the speakers cannot restore detail that the source no longer contains.
cardUpdates.noteEn: Bitrate is the amount of data used per second. With a given lossy audio format, a very low bitrate can reduce fidelity, meaning how accurately the sound is reproduced. Bitrate alone is not a universal quality score: the format, encoder, and source also matter.

cardUpdates.questionEn: What background does the comic's pretend vision test rely on?
cardUpdates.answerEn: It combines the idea of a color-vision test with large figures made from many small digits.
cardUpdates.noteEn: Real color-vision plates use differences in color to make a shape stand out. Some forms of synesthesia associate digits with colors. This black-and-white number puzzle borrows those ideas for a joke; the caption's combined diagnosis is fictional, not a valid way to assess either condition.

cardUpdates.questionEn: What does dynamic typing mean in programming?
cardUpdates.answerEn: The running program keeps track of the kind of value being used, such as a number or text, without requiring a fixed type declaration for every variable.
cardUpdates.noteEn: A variable is a name used to refer to a value. In Python, that name can first refer to a number and later to text; the values still have types, and an operation can fail if their types do not fit. Dynamic typing does not mean that types or type errors disappear.

cardUpdates.promptEs: referencias de ciencia ficción y Ron Paul
cardUpdates.questionEn: Which outside references are being compared here?
cardUpdates.answerEn: The books and television names belong to science-fiction fandom; Ron Paul is a U.S. politician associated here with the 2008 presidential campaign.
cardUpdates.noteEn: Timothy Zahn, Michael A. Stackpole, and the Corellia trilogy are references to Star Wars novels. Firefly and Battlestar Galactica are science-fiction television series. The political reference comes from the comic's 2008 setting, not from a fictional character in those stories.

cardUpdates.promptEs: armas fantásticas que brillan cerca de orcos
cardUpdates.questionEn: Why would someone expect a blue-glowing blade to detect orcs?
cardUpdates.answerEn: Tolkien's stories include blades, especially Sting, that glow blue when orcs are nearby.
cardUpdates.noteEn: That convention makes a blue glow suggest a magical warning rather than ordinary illumination. Knowing the reference explains the expectation; the comic supplies its own competing material explanation.

cardUpdates.promptEs: minimizar o maximizar una función de coste
cardUpdates.questionEn: Why does it matter whether a program minimizes or maximizes a score?
cardUpdates.answerEn: Minimizing prefers smaller scores; maximizing prefers larger ones. Adding a large positive cost discourages an outcome when minimizing, but favors it when maximizing.
cardUpdates.noteEn: A genetic algorithm repeatedly tests and selects candidate solutions using a score. A cost function assigns numbers to their outcomes. Skynet is the hostile AI from the Terminator stories; understanding the fictional name and the direction of optimization is enough to interpret the code's warning.

cardUpdates.questionEn: What relationship did Google+ have to Facebook?
cardUpdates.answerEn: Google+ was Google's competing social network, launched in 2011: similar to Facebook, but a different service.
cardUpdates.noteEn: The comparison depends on both facts being true at once. A service can offer Facebook-like functions while not being Facebook. The names identify rival products in the comic's historical setting, not two names for one network.

cardUpdates.questionEn: How can a database keep someone's entered text from becoming a command?
cardUpdates.answerEn: Use parameterized queries, which keep the query's instructions separate from the values supplied by users.
cardUpdates.noteEn: SQL is a language for working with databases. A parameterized query places user input in a separate data slot instead of pasting it into the instruction text. Checking whether input has an allowed form is validation; altering or cleaning it is often called sanitization. Neither label by itself guarantees that unsafe query construction is prevented.

cardUpdates.questionEn: What was Klout?
cardUpdates.answerEn: Klout was a service that assigned scores intended to measure people's influence on social media.
cardUpdates.noteEn: Its score was intended to summarize online reach and engagement. It measured online influence rather than directly testing a person's knowledge.

cardUpdates.questionEn: How does a Linux distribution differ from its kernel?
cardUpdates.answerEn: The kernel is the operating system's core; a Linux distribution packages that core with other software into a usable system.
cardUpdates.noteEn: Ubuntu, Debian, and Gentoo are different Linux distributions. Switching distributions changes the surrounding package and its choices. Compiling the kernel means turning its source code into an executable core, rather than merely installing an application.

cardUpdates.questionEn: What sexual innuendo is attached to the margarine?
cardUpdates.answerEn: Its greasy texture makes fetching it suggest improvised sexual lubrication.
cardUpdates.noteEn: The word is carrying an innuendo, not naming a special Spanish idiom. This is an explanation of the joke, not a claim that margarine is a suitable or safe lubricant.

cardUpdates.questionEn: What does an address beginning with 192.168 tell a network user?
cardUpdates.answerEn: It belongs to a private IPv4 address range commonly used inside local networks, rather than a globally unique public address.
cardUpdates.noteEn: The range 192.168.0.0 through 192.168.255.255 is reserved for private use. Many unrelated networks reuse it, so the prefix alone does not prove that two devices share one network. The horror allusion depends on treating the address as a clue that the danger is already inside.

cardUpdates.questionEn: Why can faster-than-light signals cause trouble for cause and effect?
cardUpdates.answerEn: In special relativity, events joined by a faster-than-light signal can be ordered differently by observers moving relative to each other.
cardUpdates.noteEn: An observer's reference frame is a way of assigning places and times to events. With suitably arranged faster-than-light signaling, one could construct a message exchange that returns information to before it was sent. That is the causality problem: an effect could precede its cause.

cardUpdates.questionEn: Which outside title does the girls-and-cups search pattern refer to?
cardUpdates.answerEn: It alludes to the title '2 Girls 1 Cup.'
cardUpdates.noteEn: The two numbers in that title become variables in the searches. Recognizing the title explains why that particular pairing stands out; no graphic description of the video is needed.

cardUpdates.questionEn: Where does the invented word shibboleet come from?
cardUpdates.answerEn: It blends shibboleth, a signal of belonging to a group, with leet, internet slang associated with technical insiders.
cardUpdates.noteEn: A shibboleth can be a word, pronunciation, or custom that distinguishes insiders from outsiders. Leet comes from 'elite' and is often written 1337 using digit substitutions. Their blend suggests an insider's identifying code.

cardUpdates.questionEn: What is SQL injection?
cardUpdates.answerEn: It happens when untrusted input is mistakenly treated as part of a database instruction instead of only as data.
cardUpdates.noteEn: SQL is a language for working with databases. If software builds a command by pasting in a user's text, that text may change the command's structure and add unintended instructions. The problem is unsafe handling of input, not the mere presence of unusual punctuation in a name.

cardUpdates.promptEs: el, la, los, las, uno o una + descripción, sin repetir el nombre
cardUpdates.questionEn: How do you say 'the small one' or 'a small one' without repeating the thing's name?
cardUpdates.answerEn: Keep the word for 'the' or 'a' and the description, but omit the noun when it is already clear.
cardUpdates.noteEn: The plus sign means put the description after the opening word. For 'the,' use el, la, los, or las to match the understood thing; for a singular 'a,' use uno for a masculine thing or una for a feminine thing when the noun is omitted. The describing word, called an adjective, still matches it: referring to a camisa, la pequeña means 'the small one.' Words such as más can qualify the description without requiring the noun to be repeated.

example.es: Quiero una taza; dame la pequeña.
example.en: I want a cup; give me the small one.

cardUpdates.promptEs: el, la, los o las + nombre opcional + más + descripción
cardUpdates.questionEn: How do you use el más or la más to say that something has the most of a quality?
cardUpdates.answerEn: Use the matching word for 'the,' name the thing if needed, then add más and the describing word.
cardUpdates.noteEn: The plus signs show the pieces in order; 'nombre opcional' means that you may omit the noun if it is already clear. El, la, los, or las matches the thing, and the describing word also matches when its form changes: la calle más larga, or la más larga when calle is understood. Más stays unchanged and marks the highest degree within the relevant group. The grammar name for this highest-degree description is a superlative.

cardUpdates.promptEs: para + acción en forma de diccionario
cardUpdates.questionEn: How do you use para to explain a purpose or what something can be used for?
cardUpdates.answerEn: Use para followed by the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cardUpdates.noteEn: The plus sign means 'followed by.' The dictionary form ends in -ar, -er, or -ir and is also called the infinitive. It names an intended action: estudio para aprender ('I study to learn') or tiempo para leer ('time for reading'). After para, that action has no separate verb ending for a new person; its doer is understood from context. To give the intended action its own explicitly stated person and changed verb, use the different para que pattern, as in para que Ana aprenda.

example.en: I study in order to learn.

cardUpdates.answerEn: are worth; have value; measure up
cardUpdates.noteEn: Valen is a present form of valer for more than one thing. It evaluates worth or usefulness, not only a price. No valen nada means they have no value; adding a comparison can make natural English use 'do not measure up.'

cardUpdates.answerEn: compared (feminine plural)
cardUpdates.noteEn: Comparadas is the feminine plural form of comparado ('compared'). Its -as ending matches the things being compared: comparado for one masculine thing, comparada for one feminine thing, comparados for a masculine or mixed group, and comparadas for a feminine group. Con introduces the reference used for comparison.

example.es: Estas cajas son pequeñas comparadas con las otras.
example.en: These boxes are small compared with the others.

earlier.noteEn: Hay introduces what exists, is present, or is available. It stays unchanged for one thing or several: hay una tienda, hay dos tiendas. English changes 'there is' to 'there are,' but Spanish does not change hay. The English 'there' in this pattern does not point to a place. Inside a description such as la tienda que hay aquí, English can instead say 'the shop that is here'; Spanish hay still introduces what is present.
